title: Keep ratios, rates and averages precise
chapter: Keep ratios, rates and averages precise
goal: Worked example: why you cannot average two averages.

scenes.visual: Two learners scoring 7 each and three learners scoring 9 each, as dots above a number line. Question: "What is the mean score of all five?"
scenes.narration: Two learners each score seven points, and three learners each score nine points. What is the mean score for all five learners?

scenes.visual: First group: 2 lots of 7 make 14. Second group: 3 lots of 9 make 27.
scenes.narration: Find the totals. The first group scores two times seven: fourteen points. The second group scores three times nine: twenty-seven points.

scenes.visual: 14 and 27 combine to 41, shared among 5 dots: 8.2 each.
scenes.narration: Together that is forty-one points for five learners. Forty-one divided by five is eight point two. The mean score is eight point two.

scenes.visual: Mark eight halfway between seven and nine, then move the balance point to 8.2, closer to the three scores of nine.
scenes.narration: Why is the mean above eight, halfway between seven and nine? Three learners score nine and two score seven, so the balance point is pulled towards nine. If you add one extra score of nine to four scores averaging eight, the mean moves one fifth of the way from eight to nine.

scenes.visual: With 2 scores of 7 and 2 scores of 9, the mean is exactly 8.
scenes.narration: If the groups were the same size, two learners at seven and two at nine, the mean would be exactly eight. The two group means now carry equal weight, so their simple average works.

scenes.visual: Line: "combine totals, then divide by everyone". Notebook prompt.
scenes.narration: Combine the totals, then divide by the total number of people. Rebuild this, then find the mean score when four learners score five each and one learner scores ten.

notebook_exercise: Four learners score 5 each and one learner scores 10. What is the mean?
